newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Portillo urges Bosnians to restore "basic links".
newsitem.headline: Portillo urges Bosnians to restore "basic links".

text.p: British Defence Minister Michael Portillo said on Monday Bosnia's rival factions must promptly restore transport and communications links to lay the ground for a lasting peace.

He told a news conference in Sarajevo the international community was encouraged at the creation of a joint inter-ethnic government but wanted to see political leadership that would bring back "the basic links at the heart of nationhood."

During his visit to the Bosnian capital, Portillo said he urged leaders from Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic to revive railway traffic, civilian flights, telephone links and open up roads across former front lines.

"Unless people are able to fly, to travel, to drive, to make telephone calls, to use the single currency within this nation we are not going to see the economic progress which is urgent in 1997," he said.
The new central government has yet to adopt a draft law on a single central bank and currency which the International Monetary Fund has demanded as a precondition for more assistance.
On his fifth tour of the former Yugoslav republic, Portillo earlier visited British troops deployed as part of the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) policing the peace agreement.
Portillo ruled out an indefinite role for NATO troops in Bosnia, saying the alliance did not foresee remaining in the country beyond SFOR's 18-month mandate, until mid-1998.

"It will not be an open-ended stay and cannot be an open- ended stay," he said. "We have made it clear that this is an 18-month mission and therefore we must look forward to enormous political progress over the next 18 months."
Last month, the 31,000-strong SFOR took over from the NATO- led Implementation Force (IFOR), which had close to 60,000 troops at its height in 1996.
The British minister met members of Bosnia's newly-formed Council of Ministers, or cabinet, on Monday as well as defence ministers from the federation and Serb republic.
Portillo said he discussed an arms control agreement with the defence ministers and expressed confidence both sides would meet weapons limits by a November 1997 deadline.
Asked about reports that a German officer would be appointed as chief of staff for the SFOR contingent, Portillo hinted that Britain would insist that the post continue to be filled by a Briton.
"I would remind you that Britain still makes the second largest contribution to the SFOR effort and the importance of that contribution must be reflected in the command structure," he said.
